\chapter{Six Verbs at the Core}
\label{ch:gu-core-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{13}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name six everyday Gujarati verbs by the neuter -\gu{વું} ending they all share, strip that ending to reach the stem, and say what I do with stem, person-ending, and the copula \gu{છે}.}

The sixth verb runs the whole chapter at once: strip the neuter -\gu{વું} from all six infinitives, hold the retroflex \gu{ણ} that Prakrit pulled back from a plain n, put the stem into hũ jāṇũ chhũ, and connect jāṇvũ to the English know it is genuinely cousin to.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hovũ]{\gu{હોવું} — \textquotedblleft{}to be,\textquotedblright{} and the neuter that names every Gujarati verb}

\label{lesson:GU-C07-hovun}



\begin{quote}
You already end a Gujarati sentence with \textbf{\gu{છે}} \emph{chhe}, \textquotedblleft{}is.\textquotedblright{} Here is the whole verb behind English \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} — and the ending that names every other Gujarati verb.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{હોવું}} — \emph{hovũ} — \textbf{to be}
\end{quote}

Left to right: \textbf{\gu{હ}} is \emph{ha}, and the sign \textbf{\gu{ો}} on it makes \emph{ho}; then \textbf{\gu{વ}} \emph{va}, with the small \textbf{\gu{ુ}} under it for \emph{vu}; and the dot \textbf{\gu{ં}} on top sends that last vowel through the nose.

Take the final piece \textbf{-\gu{વું}} \emph{-vũ} off, and the \textbf{stem} is left: \textbf{\gu{હો}-} \emph{ho-}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending is a neuter}]
Gujarati sorts words into \textbf{three} genders where Hindi next door keeps two: masculine \textbf{-o}, feminine \textbf{-ī}, and the third one, \textbf{neuter}, \textbf{-ũ} — \emph{sāro}, \emph{sārī}, \emph{sārũ}, three shapes of \textquotedblleft{}good.\textquotedblright{}

That third gender is where \textbf{-\gu{વું}} comes from. \textbf{-\gu{વું}} \emph{-vũ} is a neuter ending, so \textbf{every Gujarati verb is named in the neuter}. English names a verb by putting a word in front, \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{}; Gujarati names it by putting its third gender on the end — and hands you the stem for free every time.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{hovũ} comes from Sanskrit \emph{bhavati}, \textquotedblleft{}becomes,\textquotedblright{} on the root \emph{bhū-}. Middle Indo-Aryan thinned that \emph{bh-} to \emph{h-}, so \emph{bhavati} wore down to \emph{hoi} and then to \emph{hovũ}. The root is Indo-European, *\emph{bheu-} \textquotedblleft{}grow, become,\textquotedblright{} and English is full of it: \textbf{be}, \textbf{been}, and — through \textquotedblleft{}the place where one dwells\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{build}, \textbf{booth}, \textbf{bower}. Latin held it as \emph{futūrus}, English's \textbf{future}; Greek as \emph{phúsis}, English's \textbf{physics}.

But \textbf{\gu{છે}} \emph{chhe} is not from that root at all. It comes through Old Gujarati \emph{achhaï} from a Sanskrit verb of \textbf{dwelling, abiding} — staying put rather than becoming — and its cousins are Bengali \emph{āche} and Marathi \emph{āhe}. Hindi's \emph{hai} continues Sanskrit \emph{asti} \textquotedblleft{}is,\textquotedblright{} the same ancient verb as English \textbf{is}.

So English \textbf{is} and Hindi \emph{hai} are relatives; Gujarati \textbf{chhe} is not one of them. English plays the same trick, running \emph{be}, \emph{am}, \emph{is}, \emph{was} off several old verbs at once.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{hovũ} — to be
  \item \emph{Strip:} \textbf{hovũ} minus \textbf{-vũ} leaves the stem \textbf{ho-}
  \item \emph{Name:} the gender of \textbf{-vũ} — neuter, the third one
  \item \emph{Split:} \textbf{chhe} from a verb of dwelling; \emph{hai} and English \textbf{is} from another
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending names a Gujarati verb, and which of the three genders is it? (\textbf{-vũ}, neuter.) What is left of \emph{hovũ} once it comes off? (\textbf{Ho-}.) Does \textbf{chhe} share an ancestor with Hindi \emph{hai}? (No — \emph{hai} goes with English \textbf{is}; \emph{chhe} comes from a verb of dwelling.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%B9\%E0\%AB\%8B\%E0\%AA\%B5\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: \gu{હોવું}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%9B\%E0\%AB\%87}{Wiktionary: \gu{છે}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[javũ]{\gu{જવું} — \textquotedblleft{}to go,\textquotedblright{} and a \emph{y} that turned into a \emph{j}}

\label{lesson:GU-C07-javun}



\begin{quote}
Name the ending that titles every Gujarati verb, and take it off \emph{hovũ}. Here is the second verb wearing it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{જવું}} — \emph{javũ} — \textbf{to go}
\end{quote}

Left to right: \textbf{\gu{જ}} is \emph{ja} — it carries a built-in \emph{a}, because a Gujarati consonant with no vowel sign on it always does. Then the familiar \textbf{\gu{વું}} \emph{-vũ}. Two pieces, and you have met the second one already: \textbf{\gu{જ}} + \textbf{\gu{વું}}.

Strip the ending and the stem is \textbf{\gu{જ}-} \emph{ja-}, which stretches to \textbf{\gu{જા}-} \emph{jā-} the moment a person-ending follows it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{javũ} continues Sanskrit \emph{yāti}, \textquotedblleft{}goes,\textquotedblright{} on the root \emph{yā-}. The consonant changed on the way: \textbf{Prakrit turned word-initial Sanskrit \emph{y-} into \emph{j-}, right across the middle period.} That is a decoding tool worth keeping, because it runs through the whole vocabulary:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Sanskrit \emph{yoga} $\to$ Gujarati \emph{jog}
  \item Sanskrit \emph{yamunā} (the river) $\to$ \emph{Jamnā}
  \item Sanskrit \emph{yava} \textquotedblleft{}barley\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \emph{jav}
  \item Sanskrit \emph{yuvan} \textquotedblleft{}young\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \emph{jovān} \textquotedblleft{}a young man\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So a Gujarati word starting in \emph{j-} often has a Sanskrit \emph{y-} standing behind it.

This particular root left little in English — honest news, and better said than faked. Its clearest survival outside India is Sanskrit \emph{yāna} \textquotedblleft{}vehicle, journey,\textquotedblright{} the word inside \textbf{Mahayana}, \textquotedblleft{}the great vehicle.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: stem, then person, then the copula}]
Gujarati builds its plain present out of three pieces in a fixed order — stem, an ending that says \emph{who}, and the copula you already own:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{hũ jāũ chhũ} — I go
  \item \emph{tame jāo chho} — you go, respectfully
  \item \emph{te jāy chhe} — he goes, she goes
\end{itemize}

The copula is the piece that shifts: \emph{chhũ}, \emph{chho}, \emph{chhe}. It is \textbf{chhe} doing that work, not Hindi's \emph{hai} — the tell you traced last time. And a man and a woman say these identically: the plain present carries no gender at all.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{javũ} — to go
  \item \emph{Strip:} \textbf{javũ} minus \textbf{-vũ} leaves \textbf{ja-}
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{hũ jāũ chhũ} — I go
  \item \emph{Trace it:} Sanskrit \emph{yāti} $\to$ \textbf{javũ}, the \emph{y-} becoming \emph{j-}
  \item \emph{Apply:} \emph{yoga} $\to$ \textbf{jog}, \emph{yava} $\to$ \textbf{jav}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happened to Sanskrit \emph{y-} at the front of a word? (Prakrit made it \emph{j-}.) Which three pieces make the Gujarati present? (Stem, person-ending, copula.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I go.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hũ jāũ chhũ}.) Which of those three words is the copula, and which language does it \emph{not} match? (\emph{Chhũ}; Hindi.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%9C\%E0\%AA\%B5\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: \gu{જવું}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āvvũ]{\gu{આવવું} — \textquotedblleft{}to come,\textquotedblright{} which began as \textquotedblleft{}to reach\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C07-aavvun}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I go\textquotedblright{} in Gujarati, then strip \emph{javũ} to its stem. Here is the verb that points the other way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{આવવું}} — \emph{āvvũ} — \textbf{to come}
\end{quote}

It opens with \textbf{\gu{આ}}, the standalone letter for long \emph{ā} — Gujarati uses a full letter, not a sign, when a word begins with its vowel. Then \textbf{\gu{વ}} \emph{va}, a second \textbf{\gu{વ}}, the \textbf{\gu{ુ}}, and the nasal dot.

Two \textbf{\gu{વ}} in a row, each belonging to a different piece: the first closes the stem \textbf{\gu{આવ}-} \emph{āv-}, the second opens the ending \textbf{-\gu{વું}} \emph{-vũ} you now know by heart.

The present runs as before: \emph{hũ āvũ chhũ}, \textquotedblleft{}I come.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{āvvũ} comes through Old Gujarati \emph{āvivaũ} and Prakrit \emph{āvei} from Sanskrit \emph{āpayati}, on the root \textbf{āp-}, \textquotedblleft{}to reach, to attain.\textquotedblright{} Gujarati's \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{} is not built from \textquotedblleft{}go\textquotedblright{} at all. It is built from \textbf{arriving} — reaching the place where the speaker already is.

That root is Indo-European, and Latin holds it as \emph{apere}, \textquotedblleft{}to fasten, to reach for.\textquotedblright{} English took the family whole: \textbf{apt} (\textquotedblleft{}fitted\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{aptitude}, \textbf{adapt}, \textbf{adept}, \textbf{inept}. Put \emph{co-} \textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{} in front and Latin makes \emph{cōpula}, \textquotedblleft{}the thing that fastens two things into one\textquotedblright{} — which English borrowed in two shapes: worn down into \textbf{couple}, and kept whole as the grammarian's \textbf{copula}.

So the Gujarati verb for coming and the technical name for what \textbf{chhe} does at the end of your sentences are, far enough back, one root.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: the \emph{p} that softened to a \emph{v}}]
One regular change did most of the work between \emph{āpayati} and \emph{āvei}: \textbf{a single Sanskrit \emph{p} standing between two vowels softened to \emph{v}.} It happened right across the vocabulary, so it decodes far more than this verb:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Sanskrit \emph{dīpa} \textquotedblleft{}lamp\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \emph{dīva} $\to$ Gujarati \emph{divo}
  \item Sanskrit \emph{kūpa} \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{} $\to$ Gujarati \emph{kūvo}
\end{itemize}

And \emph{dīpa} is half of \textbf{\gu{દિવાળી}} \emph{divāḷī} — \emph{dīpa} plus \emph{āvalī}, \textquotedblleft{}a row of lamps.\textquotedblright{} The festival carries the sound change in its own name.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{āvvũ} — to come
  \item \emph{Split:} \textbf{āv-} plus \textbf{-vũ}, the two \gu{વ} belonging to different pieces
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{hũ āvũ chhũ} — I come
  \item \emph{Trace it:} Sanskrit \emph{āp-} \textquotedblleft{}reach\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textbf{āvvũ}, and $\to$ English \textbf{apt}, \textbf{couple}
  \item \emph{Apply:} \emph{dīpa} $\to$ \emph{divo}, \emph{kūpa} $\to$ \emph{kūvo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did the root behind \emph{āvvũ} originally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Reach, attain.\textquotedblright{}) What happens to a single Sanskrit \emph{p} between vowels? (It softens to \emph{v}.) Which English word for a joining verb is a cousin of \emph{āvvũ}? (\textbf{Copula}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I come.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hũ āvũ chhũ}.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%86\%E0\%AA\%B5\%E0\%AA\%B5\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: \gu{આવવું}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[khāvũ]{\gu{ખાવું} — \textquotedblleft{}to eat,\textquotedblright{} and a family that stops before English}

\label{lesson:GU-C07-khaavun}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}to come,\textquotedblright{} then name the ending it shares with every other Gujarati verb. The fourth verb takes a new letter with it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{ખાવું}} — \emph{khāvũ} — \textbf{to eat}
\end{quote}

The new letter is \textbf{\gu{ખ}}, \emph{kha}: a \emph{k} with a puff of breath straight after it. English makes that puff without noticing — hold a hand in front of your mouth and say \emph{kite}. Gujarati notices, and gives the puffed and unpuffed sounds separate letters, \textbf{\gu{ખ}} and \textbf{\gu{ક}}.

Then the long-\emph{ā} sign \textbf{\gu{ા}}, and the ending you know: \textbf{\gu{ખા}-} \emph{khā-} plus \textbf{-\gu{વું}} \emph{-vũ}. The present is \emph{hũ khāũ chhũ}, \textquotedblleft{}I eat.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{khāvũ} comes from Sanskrit \emph{khādati}, \textquotedblleft{}chews, eats.\textquotedblright{} Prakrit kept it as \emph{khādi}, and then the single \emph{d} between vowels wore away — the same erosion that has been thinning these verbs all along — leaving the bare stem \emph{khā-}.

Its sisters are all alive: Hindi \emph{khānā}, Punjabi \emph{khāṇā}, Marathi \emph{khāṇe}, Bengali \emph{khāoyā}. One verb, five modern shapes.

And there the family stops. Scholars reconstruct an Indo-European root behind \emph{khādati}, but it left nothing in English — no cousin, no borrowing, not even a worn-down one. That is worth saying out loud rather than reaching for a lookalike, because this whole method rests on hanging a new word on a word you already own, and \textbf{a cousin that is not really a cousin is worse than none at all}. Some words you take on their own terms. \emph{Khāvũ} is one of them, and its five sisters are anchor enough.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{khāvũ} — to eat, with the breath after the \emph{k}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{\gu{ખ}} puffed, \textbf{\gu{ક}} unpuffed
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{hũ khāũ chhũ} — I eat
  \item \emph{Trace it:} Sanskrit \emph{khādati} $\to$ \emph{khādi} $\to$ \textbf{khāvũ}, the \emph{d} worn away
  \item \emph{Admit:} no honest English cousin — and that is the right answer
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What separates \textbf{\gu{ખ}} from \textbf{\gu{ક}}? (A puff of breath.) Which Sanskrit verb is behind \emph{khāvũ}, and what happened to its \emph{d}? (\emph{Khādati}; it wore away between the vowels.) Which English word is its cousin? (None — and pretending otherwise would be worse than admitting it.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I eat.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hũ khāũ chhũ}.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%96\%E0\%AA\%BE\%E0\%AA\%B5\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: \gu{ખાવું}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jovũ]{\gu{જોવું} — \textquotedblleft{}to see,\textquotedblright{} one mark away from \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C07-jovun}



\begin{quote}
Two verbs back: how do you say \textquotedblleft{}to go,\textquotedblright{} and how do you say \textquotedblleft{}to eat\textquotedblright{}? The fifth verb is the nearest neighbour \emph{javũ} has.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{જોવું}} — \emph{jovũ} — \textbf{to see}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\gu{જ}} \emph{ja}, wearing the sign \textbf{\gu{ો}} that turns it into \emph{jo}; then the ending \textbf{\gu{વું}} \emph{-vũ}. The stem is \textbf{\gu{જો}-} \emph{jo-}, and the present runs as it always has: \emph{hũ joũ chhũ}, \textquotedblleft{}I see.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: one mark apart}]
Set the two words side by side and the whole difference is one small mark:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\gu{જવું}} \emph{javũ} — to go. Bare \textbf{\gu{જ}}, carrying its built-in \emph{a}.
  \item \textbf{\gu{જોવું}} \emph{jovũ} — to see. The same \textbf{\gu{જ}}, with \textbf{\gu{ો}} on it.
\end{itemize}

Add that one sign and going becomes seeing. In the mouth the contrast is just as small and just as total — \emph{ja} against \emph{jo} — so this is a pair worth saying aloud until the vowels separate cleanly. Gujarati will keep doing this: the consonants carry the word, and a single vowel mark decides which word it is.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{jovũ} continues a Prakrit verb \emph{joaï}, \textquotedblleft{}looks.\textquotedblright{} Where \emph{joaï} itself came from is genuinely unsettled, and it is more useful to say so than to pick a winner.

The usual account takes it from Sanskrit \emph{dyotate}, \textquotedblleft{}shines\textquotedblright{} — sight arriving by way of light. That is a well-worn path: Greek \emph{phaínō} \textquotedblleft{}shine\textquotedblright{} produced \emph{phainómenon}, \textquotedblleft{}a thing that shows itself,\textquotedblright{} which English borrowed as \textbf{phenomenon}, and from the same family \textbf{phantom} and \textbf{fantasy}. A second account brings in an older verb of watching and waiting for, the one behind Hindi \emph{johnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to watch out for.\textquotedblright{} The two may simply have run together; forms do that.

So: \textbf{probable, not proven.} Etymology has error bars like any other science, and a lesson that hides them is teaching you to trust the wrong things.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{jovũ} — to see
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{javũ} go, \textbf{jovũ} see — one mark, one vowel
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{hũ joũ chhũ} — I see
  \item \emph{Hedge:} \emph{jovũ} probably from \textquotedblleft{}shines\textquotedblright{} — probable, not proven
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{hovũ}, \textbf{javũ}, \textbf{āvvũ}, \textbf{khāvũ}, \textbf{jovũ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What single mark separates \emph{javũ} from \emph{jovũ}? (The \textbf{\gu{ો}} sign: \emph{ja} becomes \emph{jo}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I see.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hũ joũ chhũ}.) How settled is the origin of \emph{jovũ}? (Not settled — probably from a verb meaning \textquotedblleft{}shines,\textquotedblright{} possibly merged with one meaning \textquotedblleft{}watch out for.\textquotedblright{})

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%9C\%E0\%AB\%8B\%E0\%AA\%B5\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: \gu{જોવું}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jāṇvũ]{\gu{જાણવું} — \textquotedblleft{}to know,\textquotedblright{} a word English has been carrying all along}

\label{lesson:GU-C07-jaanvun}



\begin{quote}
Run the five you have — \emph{hovũ, javũ, āvvũ, khāvũ, jovũ} — and pull the ending off each one. The sixth is the closest of them all to English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{જાણવું}} — \emph{jāṇvũ} — \textbf{to know}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\gu{જ}} \emph{ja} with the long-\emph{ā} sign \textbf{\gu{ા}} on it gives \emph{jā}. Then a new letter: \textbf{\gu{ણ}}, an \emph{n} made with the tongue tip curled back onto the roof of the mouth — a \textbf{retroflex}, written \emph{ṇ}. Gujarati inherited a whole set of these curled sounds from Sanskrit, and you have met one before in \textbf{\gu{ળ}} \emph{ḷ}.

Then the ending. \textbf{\gu{જાણ}-} \emph{jāṇ-} plus \textbf{-\gu{વું}} \emph{-vũ}, and the present is \emph{hũ jāṇũ chhũ}, \textquotedblleft{}I know.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{jāṇvũ} comes from Sanskrit \emph{jānāti}, \textquotedblleft{}knows,\textquotedblright{} on the root \emph{jñā-}. The retroflex is Prakrit's work: a single \emph{n} between vowels was pulled back onto the roof of the mouth, so \emph{jānāti} became \emph{jāṇadi} and then \emph{jāṇvũ}.

The root is Indo-European, *\emph{gnō-} \textquotedblleft{}to know,\textquotedblright{} and English is stuffed with it.

Straight down the Germanic line: \textbf{know}, \textbf{knowledge}, \textbf{can} — which once meant \textquotedblleft{}to know how\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{cunning}, \textbf{ken}, and \textbf{uncouth}, literally \textquotedblleft{}un-known.\textquotedblright{} Borrowed from Latin \emph{(g)nōscere}: \textbf{notice}, \textbf{note}, \textbf{notion}, \textbf{cognition}, \textbf{recognize}, \textbf{acquaint}, \textbf{noble} (\textquotedblleft{}well-known\textquotedblright{}), and \textbf{ignore}, which is \textquotedblleft{}not to know.\textquotedblright{} Borrowed from Greek \emph{gnōsis}: \textbf{diagnosis}, \textbf{prognosis}, \textbf{agnostic}.

Two verbs ago the family stopped before English entirely. This one runs three dozen words deep. \emph{Jāṇvũ} is not a stranger: it is a first cousin of the plainest word English owns for the same idea, and every one of those borrowings is another peg to hang it on.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{jāṇvũ} — to know, with the tongue curled back on the \emph{ṇ}
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{hũ jāṇũ chhũ} — I know
  \item \emph{Run through:} all six — \emph{hovũ, javũ, āvvũ, khāvũ, jovũ, jāṇvũ} — stripping each stem
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{hũ jāũ chhũ}, \textbf{hũ āvũ chhũ}, \textbf{hũ khāũ chhũ}, \textbf{hũ joũ chhũ}
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{jāṇvũ} $\leftarrow$ \emph{jñā-} $\to$ English \textbf{know}, \textbf{notice}, \textbf{diagnosis}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name all six verbs and take the ending off each. (\emph{Ho-, ja-, āv-, khā-, jo-, jāṇ-}; the ending is the neuter \textbf{-vũ}.) Which English verb is the same word as \emph{jāṇvũ}? (\textbf{Know}.) What makes the \textbf{\gu{ણ}} different from a plain \emph{n}? (The tongue curls back.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I know.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hũ jāṇũ chhũ}.)

\end{tcolorbox}
